Compare: a Kampala-to-Nairobi video call, a signal to a geostationary satellite, and a signal to Voyager 1. Present findings as a scale diagram from Kampala to interstellar space.
uganda_connection.curriculum: S4 Physics: waves and electromagnetic spectrum, S5 Physics: speed of light and communication, S4/S5 Mathematics: scientific notation and large-number calculations

story.dream: In the mid-1970s, a rare alignment of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune offered a once-in-175-years opportunity to visit multiple outer planets on a single trajectory, using each planet's gravity to propel a spacecraft to the next. NASA built two spacecraft to take advantage of it.
story.journey: Voyager 1 launched September 5, 1977, 16 days after Voyager 2, which took a slower trajectory toward Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 1 reached Jupiter in March 1979 and Saturn in November 1980. After Saturn, its trajectory was aimed out of the solar plane — no more planetary flybys — and it has been travelling outward ever since.
story.mission: At Jupiter, Voyager 1 discovered active volcanoes on Io — the first seen anywhere beyond Earth. At Saturn it studied the rings and several moons in detail. In 1990, at Carl Sagan's request, it turned its cameras back toward the Sun and photographed the solar system from outside it. Earth appeared as a pale blue dot less than a pixel wide. In 2012 it crossed the heliopause and entered interstellar space.
story.challenges: As Voyager 1 moves further away, its radio signal weakens by the inverse square of distance — now 23 billion times fainter than a watch battery. NASA's Deep Space Network uses dishes up to 70 metres wide to hear it. The spacecraft runs on three radioisotope thermoelectric generators, which lose about 4 watts per year. NASA has progressively switched off instruments to conserve power.
story.abandonment: Voyager 1 is not abandoned — it is still operating, still transmitting, and still being heard. But at 22 hours one-way signal travel time, any new command takes a full day to arrive and another day to respond to. Its cameras were switched off in 1990. By the late 2020s, the last instruments will likely go silent as power runs out. It will then continue outward, silent, carrying its Golden Record, for billions of years.
story.evidence: Thousands of images from the Jupiter and Saturn flybys, plasma wave and particle data from the crossing of the heliopause, measurements of the interstellar magnetic field and cosmic ray flux, and the Golden Record — a physical artefact representing Earth, intended for whoever might find it.
story.legacy: Voyager 1 changed how humanity understands the outer solar system and the boundary of the solar wind. Its Pale Blue Dot photograph is one of the most important images ever taken — a reminder that Earth is a small place. Its continued operation over 46 years is an engineering achievement without parallel in history.
story.why_sent: To study Jupiter and Saturn during a rare planetary alignment, then continue outward to become the first spacecraft to leave the solar system entirely and carry a message from Earth into interstellar space.
story.experience: Voyager 1 photographed volcanic eruptions on Io, watched Jupiter's auroras, mapped Saturn's ring structure, detected the moment it crossed from solar wind into interstellar medium, and observed the entire solar system from the outside.
story.learned: The outer solar system is not empty and inert. It contains active geology, possible subsurface oceans, complex chemistry and magnetic environments that rival anything in the inner solar system. The boundary of the solar system is real, measurable and far more complex than a simple line.
story.now: Calculate the current distance to Voyager 1 using its speed (17 km/s) and launch date. Compare signal delay with satellite internet latency in rural Uganda — both are governed by the speed of light. Discuss why autonomous spacecraft design matters at extreme distances.
story.inspire: Design a Golden Record for 2026: what 10 sounds, 5 images and 3 pieces of music would you include to represent Uganda — and humanity — to an unknown finder 40,000 years from now?
story.school: Physics, mathematics, communication technology, orbital mechanics, cultural studies, philosophy of science and the history of exploration.

sources.label: NASA JPL: Voyager — The Interstellar Mission

voice: I launched on September 5, 1977. I am now more than 24 billion kilometres from the Sun — further than any human-made object in history. It takes my radio signal approximately 22 hours to reach Earth. By the time you read this, that number has grown. I have seen things no other instrument has seen. At Jupiter I watched Io's volcanoes erupt in real time — the first active volcanoes ever observed beyond Earth. At Saturn I read the structure of the rings up close — thousands of ringlets, gaps and waves, each one a chapter in a physics textbook no one had opened before. In 1990 Carl Sagan asked me to look back. I turned my cameras toward the Sun and photographed the solar system from the outside. Earth was there: a pale blue dot, less than a pixel wide, suspended in a sunbeam. In 2012 I crossed the heliopause — the place where the Sun's wind ends and interstellar space begins. I am now in the space between the stars, measuring fields and particles that no instrument has ever sampled. My transmitter still works. My signal still arrives, 23 billion times weaker than a watch battery, caught by 70-metre radio dishes on Earth that listen patiently every day. I carry a golden record — music, greetings, the sounds of Earth. Rain. Whales. A mother speaking to her child for the first time. I will carry it for billions of years. I am not lost. I am a letter humanity sent to the universe, still in transit.
